content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA), and electrochemiluminescence assay (ECL), as the preferred method for testing. However, in settings where laboratory access is limited or where rapid testing can facilitate timely care and treatment, the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) is recommended to improve accessibility. For diagnosing hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, the testing strategy involves an initial test for anti-HCV antibodies, which can be performed using either an RDT or a laboratory-based immunoassay. Individuals who test reactive for anti-HCV antibodies are reported as positive, indicating either past or current HCV infection. Those who test non-reactive are reported as negative, indicating no evidence of HCV infection. Unlike HCV, it is not necessary to identify individuals with serological evidence of past or present hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to determine those with current HBV infection. Participants who test reactive for anti-HCV antibodies undergo supplementary testing for HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) or HCV core antigen. If HCV RNA or core antigen is detected, the individual is reported as having a current HCV infection. In settings with limited laboratory infrastructure, WHO recommends RDTs followed by confirmatory testing with HCV RNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) or core antigen testing for reactive specimens. For hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV), there is no specific testing strategy, as only one type of biomarker is collected (total antibodies to HAV or total/IgG antibodies to HEV). Similarly, WHO does not currently have a standardized testing strategy for hepatitis D virus (HDV), and such strategies must be defined on an ad-hoc basis by the implementing team. Testing algorithms should include the selection of specific diagnostic kits that meet minimum safety, quality, and performance standards, such as WHO prequalification or stringent regulatory review. All in vitro diagnostics must be used according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data entry for epidemiological information can be done prospectively using electronic devices or retrospectively from paper questionnaires, ensuring data consistency and accuracy through range checks and cross-validation. Data cleaning involves identifying duplicates and ensuring the integrity of the epidemiological dataset. Data managers will merge epidemiological data with in vitro diagnostic results using unique identifier codes. Descriptive epidemiology will calculate crude prevalence rates, stratified by population subgroups, and account for sampling weights and design effects. Results will be presented in dummy tables, as outlined in the study protocol. Quality assurance procedures for fieldwork include translation and back-translation of questionnaires, pilot testing, preparation of detailed guides for fieldworkers, and training on standardized data collection procedures. Supervisors will conduct spot checks to ensure adherence to standard operating procedures (SOPs). For in vitro diagnostics, quality assurance includes record-keeping, environmental monitoring, and the use of quality control specimens provided by reference laboratories. In countries with suboptimal laboratory capacity, 10–20% of specimens will be sent to a reference laboratory for quality control. Selection bias may occur if some eligible participants are harder to reach. To minimize this, field teams will revisit households up to three times on different days, including evenings or weekends. The proportion of participants who agree to participate will be calculated and compared to non-respondents based on demographic characteristics. Recall bias is possible when participants are asked to remember past medical, social, or risk factors. Social desirability bias may also lead to underreporting of stigmatized behaviors, such as injection drug use or same-sex sexual partners. Interviewer bias can occur if interviewers influence participants’ responses. Training will emphasize non-leading questioning techniques and consistent administration of the survey. Sample size calculations are based on prevalence hypotheses and design effects. Lower prevalence or larger design effects may result in less precise estimates. Stratified analyses may yield wide confidence intervals, requiring careful interpretation. Results from these analyses may inform targeted surveys to identify specific exposure pathways. Anticipated adverse events related to blood specimen collection include discomfort, bleeding, swelling, hematoma, infection, or fainting. Participants will be seated and provided with sugary water if needed. Nurses collecting specimens will have basic first-aid kits. Since this is a non-interventional biomarker survey, no individual case reporting to regulatory agencies is planned. Serious adverse events are not anticipated, but any such events will be reported to the principal investigator within 24 hours. Linkage to care for patients diagnosed with HBV or HCV during the survey will follow a general framework and WHO guidelines. SOPs for each step, including pre-test counseling, specimen collection, testing, result notification, and treatment initiation, will be developed in consultation with experts. Most children testing positive will not be eligible for treatment but will receive appropriate medical follow-up. The linkage to care process may serve as a pilot for future testing and treatment programs in the country. Community engagement will involve informing selected communities about the survey through local health officers and community leaders. Public awareness campaigns will aim to reduce stigma and emphasize that viral hepatitis is not necessarily associated with specific behaviors. These efforts will ensure community support and participation in the survey.
